title: Declaration of Independence — Human Equality and the Right of Revolution
author: Thomas Jefferson et al. (Committee of Five, with revisions by the Second Continental Congress)
source: Declaration of Independence, engrossed parchment copy, adopted by the Second Continental Congress, July 4, 1776, and signed August 2, 1776. National Archives and Records Administration, Washington, D.C.
selection_notes: The second paragraph of the Declaration of Independence, often called the 'preamble' or the philosophical preamble. This passage contains the foundational political philosophy of the American founding: the self-evident truth of human equality, the doctrine of unalienable rights, the social contract theory of government (legitimate government derives its just powers from consent), the right of revolution, and the prudential constraints on exercising that right. The extract is a continuous, tightly reasoned argument that moves from metaphysical premises (creation, equality, rights) through political theory (government by consent) to a practical conclusion (the conditions under which revolution is justified). The passage is arguably the most influential statement of liberal democratic principles in political history and contains complex semantic structures: universal quantifiers ('all men'), causal relations ('to secure these rights'), modality ('should not be changed'), conditionals ('whenever...'), and rhetorical contrast ('Prudence...indeed will dictate...But when...').
normalization_notes: Text follows the engrossed parchment copy as transcribed by the National Archives. Original capitalization preserved (e.g., 'Life', 'Liberty', 'Happiness', 'Governments', 'Men', 'People', 'Safety', 'Object', 'Despotism', 'Guards'). Original spelling preserved including 'unalienable' (not 'inalienable' — this is the spelling on the parchment), 'shewn' (not 'shown'), and 'pursuing invariably' (no comma). The em-dashes separating clauses are original to the parchment text. The paragraph break after 'future security' is the paragraph boundary in the original parchment.
